shows: Price levels worked out from the options market: the call wall, the put wall and the zero gamma line. GEX (gamma exposure) estimates how much hedging dealers must do as price moves.
A wall is a strike with unusually large exposure. Zero gamma is the price where the estimate flips from positive to negative.
use: Some traders mark these levels before the session as places where price may react or move faster.
Some compare today's price with the zero gamma line to see which side of it the market is trading on.
limits: It is an estimate built from open interest and an assumed dealer position, not a fact about what dealers hold.
It does not say price will stop at a level or which way it will go.

shows: Net gamma exposure at every strike, snapshot by snapshot, painted under the candles. Mint is positive, red is negative, and clear means close to zero.
A status note shows how many minutes ago the data was updated.
use: Look at where the strongest bands sit and how they moved during the session.
Compare the bands with where price spent its time, to learn how the two relate.
limits: It shows an estimate of exposure, not orders or trades.
It cannot show changes inside one snapshot, and it only covers the period that was recorded.

shows: The price range the options market implies for an expiry (0DTE means expiring today), drawn as a shaded box with dashed edges.
The data is shown with an "updated X min ago" note.
use: Some traders use the edges as a rough sense of how far price is expected to travel by the expiry.
Some use it to size expectations before the open, for example whether a move is large or small against the range.
limits: It is the range options pricing implies, not a forecast. Price often finishes outside it.
Nothing is drawn in bar replay, because the range belongs to today.

shows: Two running lines in a lower pane: net call premium (green) and net put premium (red) since the 9:30 ET open. Premium is the money paid for options contracts.
A status note shows how many minutes ago it was updated.
use: Watch whether call or put money is building faster as the day goes on.
Compare the lines with the candles to see whether options money and price agree.
limits: The bought versus sold split is estimated from volume and quotes, so it can be wrong on single trades.
It shows money, not intent: a put can be a hedge as easily as a bet.

shows: Bubbles on candles where call premium (green, above) or put premium (red, below) was unusually large. Premium is the money paid for contracts.
Bigger bubbles mean more premium. Tap a bubble for the details.
use: Spot bars where options money was heavy and read the candle around it.
Compare call and put bubbles across the day to see which side was more active.
limits: Strike and expiry are not in the data, so a bubble does not tell you which contract it was.
Premium is estimated, and a large trade can be a hedge rather than a view.

shows: Large stock trades reported off the public exchanges ("dark pool" or off-exchange trades), drawn at the price and time they printed. Dot size follows dollar value, and $10M or more is highlighted.
The chart shows when the list was last updated.
use: See where big blocks traded relative to your levels and recent candles.
Open the Dark pool list for the time, price and size of each print.
limits: A print does not say whether the buyer or the seller started the trade.
The list is updated every 2 hours on US trading days. Only US stocks and ETFs on a set list are covered.

shows: Horizontal lines at the average price of each week's off-exchange trading (trades away from the public exchanges). Thicker lines mean more shares.
It uses public weekly volume data.
use: Treat the lines as reference prices where a lot of off-exchange volume built up.
Compare them with your own support and resistance.
limits: A level is a weekly average price, not a single trade.
The weekly data arrives with a lag of several weeks, so recent weeks are missing.

shows: A lower pane with the daily percentage of a stock's volume that was traded off the public exchanges.
It uses public daily volume data.
use: See whether the off-exchange share is high or low compared with recent days.
Compare spikes in the share with big days on the price chart.
limits: It shows a share of volume, not the direction of the trades.
Daily charts only, for listed stocks and ETFs in the data.

shows: One past session's key levels on the chart: previous day high, low and close, the open, the gap, the opening range and the initial balance. A marker shows where the studied outcome happened.
It is opened from a Market Stats page.
use: Use it to look at one example day from the statistics, with every level drawn.
Step through several dates to see how the same levels looked on different days.
limits: The statistics are how often something happened in the past, not a forecast.
On its own, without a Market Stats link, it has no session to draw.

shows: Each candle split by price: how much traded at the bid (sellers) and at the ask (buyers) on every row, with the resting order book size at the close beside it.
Futures order book data (L2) is a Pro feature.
use: Look for rows where one side clearly dominated, or where a lot of size was resting.
Compare the numbers with where the candle closed.
limits: Resting size is a snapshot at the bar close; orders can come and go inside the bar.
It describes what traded, not what will trade next.

shows: Each candle split by price, with the volume traded at the bid (sellers) and at the ask (buyers) on every row.
Order flow tools are a Pro feature.
use: Look for price rows where one side clearly outweighed the other (an imbalance).
Compare the totals with how the candle closed.
limits: It needs per-trade data and works on supported symbols only.
It shows what already traded, not what will trade next.

shows: Bubbles for the largest aggressive orders (an aggressive order takes the price on the other side instead of waiting). A letter says what the order book did: W hit a resting wall, C consumed several levels, P the book was pulled.
Buyers and sellers have separate colours.
use: See where large orders landed and how the book reacted.
Filter by size to keep only the biggest.
limits: Fills are joined into one order by timing and price, so the tags are estimates.
A big order does not mean price will follow it.

shows: A pane with two numbers per bar. Trade delta is volume bought at the ask minus volume sold at the bid. Book delta is the size added or removed on the bid and the ask.
Together they show what traded and how resting orders changed.
use: Compare delta with the candle: did price move the way the delta pointed?
Look for bars where trade delta and book delta disagree.
limits: Delta describes one bar and can flip the next.
Resting orders can be pulled at any time, so book delta is a snapshot of intent, not a commitment.

shows: The running total of trade delta plus book delta, reset each session. Delta is buying minus selling volume.
A dashed line can show the trade-only total for comparison.
use: Watch whether the total rises or falls with price, or moves against it.
Compare the two lines to see how much the order book added.
limits: The total depends on where it was reset.
A rising total does not mean price must rise.

shows: Marks bars that push past a recent swing high or low on a volume spike, but only when the order book shows liquidity on that side was pulled or taken through several levels.
Swept lows are green and swept highs red.
use: Review where price took out a recent extreme and what happened after.
Show the unconfirmed sweeps as hollow marks to compare.
limits: A mark describes one bar. It is not a signal.
The book confirmation is based on a snapshot of the order book.

shows: Traded volume at each price for the session, with the average resting bid and ask size at that price beside it.
It needs the futures order book (L2), a Pro feature.
use: See where volume traded and where orders waited.
Compare busy prices with the current price.
limits: Resting size is an average and can change at any time.
It describes the session so far, not what comes next.

shows: A ladder on the right of the price chart. Each row shows buying minus selling volume (delta) at that price for the visible part of the chart.
It needs the futures order book (L2), a Pro feature.
use: Find the prices where buying or selling stood out.
Scroll the chart and watch the ladder follow the visible range.
limits: It covers only what is visible on screen.
A heavy row is something that happened, not a promise about the next move.

shows: The order book as a heatmap: size resting at every price over time. Soft blue is thin, and the biggest resting orders turn yellow, orange and red.
Trade balls and the order book ladder are drawn on top.
use: See where large orders waited, how long they stayed and where they disappeared.
Adjust Smooth and Contrast to make bands easier to read.
limits: Resting orders can be added or pulled at any moment. The map shows what was there.
It has no buy or sell buttons and says nothing about direction.

shows: The futures order book painted behind your candles. Brighter bands are prices with a lot of size waiting. A band that ends means the orders were pulled or traded.
DOM stands for depth of market, the list of resting orders.
use: Look for big bands near price and see whether price stalls, passes or removes them.
Switch looks and depth bars to find the view that reads best.
limits: It shows resting orders, which can disappear before price arrives.
The chart shows when the book was last updated (for example "updated 2s ago").

shows: Only the unusually large resting orders in the futures book that stayed in place, each with its size. Walls that vanish can be tagged as pulled (cancelled) or filled (traded through).
It is the heatmap with walls only.
use: Use it to keep the chart clean while still seeing the biggest levels.
Review how price behaved when it met a wall.
limits: A wall is resting interest at one moment and can be pulled at any time.
Pulled versus filled is worked out from trades at that price, so it is an estimate.

shows: A pane showing whether the bid side or the ask side of the book is heavier. One line uses only the best bid and ask; an optional line weighs ten levels each side.
It needs the futures order book (L2), a Pro feature.
use: Watch the line cross zero to see which side was heavier.
Compare it with price to learn how the two relate.
limits: Resting size can be pulled at any time, so the line can flip fast.
It describes the book, not who will win the next trade.

shows: How many resting levels near price change every second, drawn in a pane and coloured calm, normal or fast.
Calm, normal and fast are compared with the same session.
use: See when the book becomes busy or goes quiet.
Compare fast periods with news or session opens.
limits: The labels are relative to the session, not fixed numbers.
A busy book does not say which way price will go.

shows: A pane with the resting bid size and ask size within a set distance of price, and the difference between them.
It needs the futures order book (L2), a Pro feature.
use: Check which side has more size close to price.
Watch how the balance changes as price moves.
limits: Resting orders can be pulled at any time.
More size on one side does not mean price will move away from it.

shows: An R marker when a resting level is hit by aggressive orders and then gets its size back within a few seconds. Green is a refilled bid, red a refilled ask.
use: Look at where refills happened and what price did around them.
Use it to study how the book behaves at busy levels.
limits: A refill can come from many small orders, so it is a hint, not proof of one large order.
It describes the past, not a signal.

shows: A thin strip under the candles that labels the book tight, normal or wide, based on how spread out the resting size is around price.
use: See when the book thins out or crowds in near price.
Compare the strip with how fast candles are moving.
limits: Tight, normal and wide are relative to the current session.
It does not predict a move; it describes the book.

shows: Short lines and labels at the few biggest orders in the book right now, with their size and how long each has rested.
use: Spot big orders sitting near price and how long they have stayed.
Watch whether they remain or disappear as price approaches.
limits: Orders can be pulled at any time.
It shows the book at this moment, not a plan by any trader.

shows: Markers on big resting walls when something happens to them: a filled square means eaten, a hollow H means held or refilled, a grey x means pulled.
use: Study what usually happens when price reaches a big wall.
Compare eaten, held and pulled walls on the same session.
limits: Pulled versus eaten is worked out from trades at the price, so it is an estimate.
A marker describes what happened, not what comes next.

shows: A pane that counts absorption, iceberg hints and stop runs over the session, with buy-side events going up and sell-side events going down.
Absorption means heavy trading at a price without price moving. An iceberg is a large order shown in small pieces.
use: See which side has shown more of these events so far.
Compare the count with price to learn how they line up.
limits: These are hints from trades and book changes; hidden orders cannot be seen directly.
A higher count does not predict direction.

shows: Zones where three or more stacked price rows showed one side clearly outweighing the other (an imbalance). The zone extends right until price trades through it.
use: Use the zones as reference areas to study how price behaved when it came back.
Change the row size to see fewer, wider zones.
limits: It needs per-trade data, so it works on supported symbols only.
A zone is a record of past trading, not a promise of a reaction.

shows: Marks bars where heavy aggressive volume hit one price but price barely moved, and extends that level right until a bar closes through it.
use: Look at the marked levels and see how price reacted when it returned.
Hide broken levels to keep the chart clean.
limits: It needs per-trade data, so it works on supported symbols only.
It flags past bars. It does not say a level will hold.

shows: A lower pane that compares each bar's volume (effort) with its range (result). High effort with low result is flagged amber; low effort with high result is flagged violet.
use: Look for bars where a lot traded but price went nowhere, or the reverse.
Use the flags to review those bars on the chart.
limits: Bars are compared with their own recent average, so the same volume can flag differently on different days.
A flag is a description of a bar, not a signal.

shows: How much time price spent at each level in a session, built from 30-minute letters (TPO means time price opportunity). It marks the initial balance, the point of control (POC, the busiest price), the 70% value area and single prints.
use: See where the session found acceptance and where it moved quickly.
Compare today's profile with previous days.
limits: It is built from candles, so it shows time at price, not volume.
A profile describes a session that has happened, not the next one.

shows: The crypto order book painted behind your candles. Brighter bands mean more size waiting at that price. A band that ends means the orders were pulled or traded.
DOM stands for depth of market.
use: Look for large bands near price and watch how price meets them.
Try the different looks to find one that reads clearly.
limits: Resting orders can be added or pulled at any moment.
History depends on how long the book has been recorded for that symbol.

shows: A map of resting order-book size over time: the glow runs from deep blue (small) to yellow, orange and red (the biggest). A price line, trade bubbles, a book ladder and volume bars sit on top.
use: See where large orders waited and where they were removed.
Use the contrast and size filters to find the view you like.
limits: It describes resting orders and prints. It does not predict anything.
Futures depth for this tool is limited for now; crypto works for Pro members.

shows: Bubbles on bars whose volume was at least twice the recent average. Up candles get a green bubble at the high, down candles a red bubble at the low, with a label such as 3.2x.
use: Spot unusually busy bars quickly.
Look at the candle and the next few bars to see how price reacted.
limits: It marks whole bars, not single trades.
Heavy volume does not say whether buyers or sellers won.

shows: Three lines from the last full session: the point of control (POC, the busiest price) as a solid line, and the value area high and low (VAH and VAL, the range holding about 70% of volume) as dashed lines.
use: Some traders use them as reference prices for today.
Compare where today opens with the previous day's value area.
limits: They are built from candle volume, not individual trades.
They describe yesterday. Price can ignore them.

shows: One volume profile per session: how much traded at each price. The POC (busiest price) is orange, and the value area high and low (about 70% of volume) are dashed lines.
use: See where each session did most of its trading.
Compare one session's profile with the next.
limits: It is built from candle volume, not trade by trade.
Intraday charts only.

shows: The volume-weighted average price (VWAP) from a bar you choose, with bands one, two and three standard deviations above and below. VWAP is the average price paid, weighted by volume.
use: Anchor it to a swing, an event or a session start and see where price sits against the average.
Add more than one copy with different anchors.
limits: It uses candle prices, not every trade.
The anchor stays where you put it until you change it.

shows: Horizontal bands behind the candles at the prices where the most volume built up in the visible range. Green means up candles contributed more, red means down candles did.
use: Spot prices where a lot of trading happened.
Zoom to a different range to see how the bands change.
limits: It is built from candle volume and range, not trades at each price.
It does not show resting orders; use the depth heatmaps for that.

shows: Dashed vertical lines at scheduled releases such as CPI, FOMC, NFP and GDP, with a countdown chip when the next one is close.
use: Know when a release is due before you enter a trade.
Tap a line to see the forecast and previous values.
limits: Times and values come from a calendar feed and can change.
It marks events. It does not say how price will react.

shows: RSI (relative strength index) is a line from 0 to 100 that compares recent up moves with down moves over a set number of bars.
use: Some traders watch the 70 and 30 lines for stretched moves.
Some watch for the line to disagree with price (divergence).
limits: A high or low reading can last a long time in a strong trend.
It uses past prices only.

shows: MACD (moving average convergence divergence) shows the gap between a fast and a slow moving average, a signal line, and a histogram of the difference.
use: Some traders watch the lines cross or the histogram change size.
Some use it to compare momentum between swings.
limits: It lags price, because it is built from averages.
Crossovers are frequent in sideways markets.

shows: VWAP is the average price traded so far, weighted by volume, with optional bands based on standard deviation (a measure of spread).
use: Some traders watch whether price is above or below VWAP during the session.
Bands show how stretched price is from the average.
limits: It resets on the anchor you choose, so the starting point matters.
It uses candle prices and volume.

shows: SuperTrend draws a line that follows price at a distance set by ATR (average true range, the typical size of a bar). Its colour flips when price closes through it.
use: Some traders use the line as a trailing reference for a trend.
Compare the flips with your own read of the market.
limits: It lags, and flips often in sideways markets.
It is a description of past price, not a signal.

shows: Bollinger Bands draw a moving average with bands set a number of standard deviations (a measure of spread) above and below it.
use: Some traders watch the bands tighten and widen to see volatility change.
Some compare price with the bands to see how stretched it is.
limits: Touching a band does not mean price will reverse.
Default settings are a starting point, not a rule.
